title: A Systematic Review of Optimization Algorithms for Structural Health Monitoring and Optimal Sensor Placement

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Structural Health Monitoring and Sensor Placement Optimization
subsections.subsection_title: Foundations of Structural Health Monitoring and Sensor Placement Optimization - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Structural health monitoring (SHM) is broadly concerned with inferring the condition of a structure from measured response data so that damage can be detected, localized, assessed, and tracked over time. Foundational SHM literature frames this process as the acquisition of data, extraction of damage-sensitive features, and statistical or model-based interpretation under operational and environmental variability ref [9], ref [26], ref [55]. This definition is especially important for sensor placement studies because the value of a sensor configuration depends on the specific inference task to be supported rather than on measurement coverage alone.

A common conceptual basis for SHM is the hierarchy of monitoring objectives, ranging from damage detection to localization, severity quantification, and prognosis or decision support. Reviews of SHM methods emphasize that increasing diagnostic ambition generally requires richer sensing, better observability of structural states, and more robust algorithms for handling noise, uncertainty, and changing boundary conditions ref [26], ref [56]. From an implementation perspective, the gap between laboratory demonstrations and industrial deployment has further highlighted practical requirements such as scalability, reliability, maintainability, and actionable outputs for asset management ref [15].

These SHM foundations directly motivate optimal sensor placement (OSP). OSP is not merely a geometric layout problem; it is a decision problem linking sensing resources to identifiability, information content, and monitoring performance under budgetary and operational constraints ref [16], ref [55]. Comparative studies using standard data sets also show that evaluation criteria and benchmark conditions strongly influence conclusions about monitoring effectiveness, underscoring the need for reproducible formulations when optimization algorithms are reviewed ref [28]. Accordingly, this survey treats SHM objectives, sensing assumptions, and performance metrics as the essential context for comparing OSP strategies ref [16], ref [26].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Structural Health Monitoring and Sensor Placement Optimization
subsections.subsection_title: Foundations of Structural Health Monitoring and Sensor Placement Optimization - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A core foundation for structural health monitoring is the measurement system itself: SHM performance depends not only on damage-sensitive algorithms but also on sensor type, durability, communication architecture, and compatibility with the monitored structure. Reviews of vibration-based SHM emphasize that sensing choices must be aligned with the target response quantity—typically acceleration, strain, displacement, or modal properties—and with the relevant technical codes and operational constraints ref [10], ref [23]. This systems view is especially important because OSP is meaningful only relative to a specific sensing modality, data quality requirement, and monitoring objective.

The SHM literature highlights a broad spectrum of sensing technologies with distinct trade-offs. Fibre optic and Bragg grating sensors offer high sensitivity, multiplexing capability, and suitability for distributed strain monitoring, making them attractive for composites, concrete, and other demanding environments ref [41], ref [31]. Passive wireless sensors reduce cabling burden and facilitate scalable deployments, though they introduce power, interrogation, and communication-range considerations that affect practical network design ref [40]. In large bridge applications, integrated smart monitoring systems combine multiple sensor classes to capture global and local behavior under environmental and traffic loading, illustrating that sensor heterogeneity is often necessary in real structures ref [20]. Similar implementation lessons are reported for multi-story buildings, where installation accessibility, maintenance, synchronization, and data management strongly influence sensor network feasibility ref [56].

These characteristics directly shape OSP problem formulation. Placement cannot be treated as a purely geometric exercise; it must consider sensor accuracy, sampling strategy, long-term reliability, redundancy, and the clinical purpose of monitoring—diagnosis, prognosis, or decision support ref [46]. Consequently, optimization criteria in SHM should be interpreted in the context of the chosen sensing technology and infrastructure, since practical deployability may favor robust, maintainable configurations over theoretically maximal information gain ref [20], ref [40], ref [56].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Structural Health Monitoring and Sensor Placement Optimization
subsections.subsection_title: Foundations of Structural Health Monitoring and Sensor Placement Optimization - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A foundational issue for SHM-oriented sensor placement is the relationship between damage mechanisms, sensing modality, and measurable response. SHM systems may rely on global dynamic responses, local electromechanical signatures, guided/acoustic waves, or data-driven feature representations, each offering different spatial sensitivity, frequency content, and operational requirements. Broad surveys of SHM emphasize that no single sensing principle is universally dominant; instead, the monitoring objective and expected damage scenario largely determine the appropriate sensing architecture ref [10], ref [17].

For civil infrastructure, vibration-based monitoring remains the most established paradigm because modal properties, transmissibility, and response statistics can be collected at structural scale and linked to damage detection and condition assessment workflows ref [14], ref [25]. However, vibration measurements are typically more sensitive to global stiffness changes than to incipient local defects, which motivates complementary high-frequency techniques. Impedance-based SHM using piezoelectric transducers offers strong local sensitivity for small cracks, debonding, and joint degradation, while piezoelectric acoustic-wave methods support active interrogation with finer damage localization capability ref [43], ref [48]. These distinctions are central to OSP because optimal locations for low-frequency accelerometers need not coincide with those for PZT patches or wave-based actuators/sensors ref [17], ref [48].

Recent SHM literature also shows that sensor placement quality should be evaluated not only by information capture but by downstream diagnostic reliability. Machine-learning-based SHM and NDE pipelines depend strongly on feature richness, data balance, and sensor coverage, making placement decisions inseparable from classification, localization, and prognosis performance ref [53]. In parallel, reliability metrics such as probability of detection, localization, and sizing provide a more operational basis for comparing sensing layouts under uncertainty ref [56]. Consequently, OSP in this review is treated as a modality-aware and performance-driven design problem, where sensing technology, damage observability, and decision reliability must be optimized jointly rather than independently ref [10], ref [56].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Structural Health Monitoring and Sensor Placement Optimization
subsections.subsection_title: Foundations of Structural Health Monitoring and Sensor Placement Optimization - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A practical foundation for optimal sensor placement must account not only for observability or damage sensitivity, but also for deployment constraints that dominate real installations. Fielded SHM systems face limits associated with power supply, communication reliability, environmental robustness, maintenance access, calibration drift, and long-term data management, all of which can invalidate placements that are optimal only in simulation ref [26], ref [39], ref [50]. Consequently, OSP in practice is better formulated as a constrained, multi-criteria design problem in which sensing performance is balanced against installation cost, survivability, network connectivity, and lifecycle operability ref [26], ref [16], ref [39].

These implementation realities are especially important in wireless and distributed SHM architectures. Hierarchical active-sensing networks illustrate how sensing topology, onboard processing, and communication burden are coupled, implying that sensor location decisions should be co-designed with network architecture rather than treated as an isolated geometric problem ref [43]. Power autonomy further reshapes feasible placements: energy-harvesting strategies can relax battery constraints in aerospace and remote systems, but they also introduce spatial dependence on harvestable energy sources and duty-cycling requirements ref [20]. Likewise, low-power wireless modalities such as RFID-based strain sensing expand deployment flexibility, yet their read range, interrogation conditions, and measurement resolution impose additional placement trade-offs ref [53].

Beyond physical deployment, scalable SHM also depends on benchmarked evaluation and digital information management. Benchmark studies and guideline-oriented assessments are valuable because they provide common problem definitions and performance criteria for comparing OSP algorithms under realistic assumptions ref [16]. In parallel, virtual environments for visualizing sensor networks, data streams, and metadata support traceability of sensor configuration decisions and help manage system complexity over time ref [48]. Taken together, these considerations show that the foundations of OSP are inseparable from system implementation, validation protocols, and operational decision support in large-scale SHM ref [39], ref [48], ref [50].

subsections.section_title: Foundations of Structural Health Monitoring and Sensor Placement Optimization
subsections.subsection_title: Foundations of Structural Health Monitoring and Sensor Placement Optimization - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A final foundation for this review is the recognition that SHM performance is jointly determined by sensor technology, network architecture, and power availability, not only by the optimization algorithm used for placement. Reviews of SHM sensing systems emphasize that accelerometers, strain gauges, piezoelectric transducers, fiber-optic sensors, displacement sensors, and wireless sensor nodes differ markedly in bandwidth, sensitivity, durability, communication burden, and installation cost; these characteristics directly constrain what an OSP formulation can reasonably optimize ref [30], ref [50]. Consequently, sensor placement should be interpreted as a co-design problem in which sensing modality, interrogation hardware, and deployment environment shape the feasible search space ref [14], ref [30].

This systems perspective is especially important because SHM objectives range from vibration-based global assessment to feature extraction for statistical pattern recognition. Vibration-based SHM relies on modal observability, dynamic response quality, and sensitivity to damage-induced changes, making placement criteria such as independence, information content, and identifiability central to network design ref [20], ref [14]. In contrast, data-driven SHM framed through statistical pattern recognition places stronger emphasis on representative measurements, environmental variability, and stable feature generation, implying that optimal locations are those that support robust discrimination rather than only maximal modal coverage ref [17]. Thus, the merit of an OSP strategy must be judged relative to the downstream inference task.

Practical deployment further introduces energy, maintenance, and longevity constraints, particularly for wireless SHM systems. Energy harvesting technologies have been proposed to reduce battery dependence, but harvested power is intermittent and application-specific, which links node placement to local vibration, solar, wind, or thermal availability as well as communication duty cycles ref [51]. Together with the implementation challenges documented in sensor-system reviews—such as calibration drift, synchronization, data loss, and environmental exposure—these considerations justify evaluating optimization algorithms not only by objective-function value, but also by scalability, robustness to uncertainty, and compatibility with realistic sensing infrastructures ref [30], ref [50], ref [51].

subsections.section_title: Optimization Problem Formulations for Sensor Placement and SHM Design
subsections.subsection_title: Optimization Problem Formulations for Sensor Placement and SHM Design - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A first class of formulations treats optimal sensor placement as an information-maximization problem over a finite set of candidate locations. In this view, the decision variables are binary placement indicators, and the objective is to maximize the informativeness of measured responses for identification, damage classification, or state estimation. Review studies consistently frame these objectives through Fisher information, entropy, mutual information, determinant- or rank-based metrics of observability, and related criteria that seek to reduce redundancy while preserving sensitivity to structural changes ref [16], ref [55]. Within broader SHM architectures, such formulations are tied to the statistical pattern recognition paradigm, where sensor layouts are judged by their ability to support feature extraction, discrimination between healthy and damaged states, and robust decision-making under environmental and operational variability ref [9], ref [26].

In practice, these formulations are rarely unconstrained. Large-scale civil structures impose geometric accessibility limits, installation and maintenance restrictions, power and communication constraints, and the need to guarantee coverage of critical components rather than only globally informative locations ref [56], ref [15]. Consequently, the optimization problem is often expressed as a constrained combinatorial design task: maximize information or detectability subject to bounds on sensor count, feasible mounting regions, network connectivity, durability, and cost ref [16], ref [56]. Such constraints are especially important for moving from laboratory-optimal layouts to deployable SHM systems, a gap repeatedly emphasized in reviews of industrial implementation and fielded monitoring programs ref [15], ref [26].

A related modeling choice concerns whether the formulation is single-objective or multi-objective. Surveyed SHM literature shows a growing preference for multi-criteria statements that jointly balance information gain, damage sensitivity, redundancy reduction, uncertainty mitigation, and lifecycle practicality, rather than optimizing a purely mathematical criterion in isolation ref [55], ref [16]. This broader formulation is consistent with system-level SHM perspectives, where sensor placement is only one design layer coupled to data analytics, inspection planning, and operational decision support ref [9], ref [15].

subsections.section_title: Optimization Problem Formulations for Sensor Placement and SHM Design
subsections.subsection_title: Optimization Problem Formulations for Sensor Placement and SHM Design - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A second major class of formulations casts sensor placement as a sparsity-constrained inference problem, where the objective is not only to maximize sensitivity to damage but also to reconstruct structural states from incomplete measurements. In this view, optimization seeks a sensor subset that preserves identifiability under compressive or underdetermined sampling, often by minimizing reconstruction error, maximizing posterior relevance, or enforcing sparse representations of damage features and wave responses. Robust Bayesian compressive sensing is particularly relevant because it embeds uncertainty and noise modeling directly into the recovery process, making placement quality dependent on both sensing geometry and posterior confidence ref [9]. Related sparse-sampling formulations for guided-wave SHM use outlier separability and defect discriminability as optimization criteria, showing that sparse layouts can remain effective when the objective is defined in terms of anomaly detection rather than full-field reconstruction ref [44].

These formulations are closely tied to application-specific SHM architectures. Benchmark-oriented studies emphasize that optimal layouts must support reliable feature extraction under realistic variability, including changing environmental and operational conditions, which effectively introduces robustness terms or multi-scenario constraints into the optimization problem ref [17]. Software-integrated SHM platforms similarly motivate formulations that jointly consider estimation quality, data fusion, and computational tractability, rather than isolated sensor-count minimization ref [51]. More broadly, prescriptive and overview papers in SHM argue that optimization should be aligned with the intended diagnostic task—detection, localization, prognosis, or model updating—because the mathematical objective changes substantially across these use cases ref [46], ref [23].

In practical deployments, sparsity-based and task-driven formulations are further constrained by installation feasibility, communication topology, maintenance access, and long-term operability. Case studies on long-span arch bridges and multi-story buildings show that the nominally optimal sensor set is often adjusted to satisfy cable routing, power supply, redundancy, and field calibration requirements, yielding constrained or multi-objective formulations that balance informativeness against implementability ref [20], ref [56]. Consequently, modern SHM design problems are increasingly posed as joint optimization of sensing, inference, and system operation, rather than as purely geometric placement problems ref [23], ref [46].

subsections.section_title: Optimization Problem Formulations for Sensor Placement and SHM Design
subsections.subsection_title: Optimization Problem Formulations for Sensor Placement and SHM Design - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A third class of formulation extends optimal sensor placement from estimation quality alone to reliability- and decision-oriented SHM design. In this view, objective functions are defined in terms of probability of detection, localization, and sizing, so that sensor layouts are selected to maximize diagnosability under realistic uncertainty rather than only modal independence or information entropy ref [56]. Such formulations are particularly relevant when SHM is used for condition assessment and risk-informed maintenance, where the value of a sensor is measured by its contribution to dependable inference about damage existence, position, and severity ref [51], ref [56].

These reliability-centered objectives are often embedded in life-cycle optimization. For bridge and ship structures, SHM system design has been coupled with life-cycle performance assessment, where sensor placement and monitoring policies are chosen to reduce uncertainty in deterioration models, improve maintenance timing, and minimize expected long-term risk or cost ref [33], ref [35]. In these settings, the optimization variables may include not only sensor locations, but also sensing frequency, inspection integration, and data-assimilation strategies, with constraints derived from operational availability and management requirements ref [33], ref [35], ref [51].

Practical SHM formulations further incorporate network-level constraints that materially change the feasible design space. Wireless architectures motivate objectives balancing sensing benefit against communication burden, latency, fault tolerance, and multi-scale coverage ref [28]. Sensor fault management introduces robustness terms that reward redundancy or reconfigurability under node malfunction ref [16], while energy-harvesting-enabled systems add power neutrality and duty-cycle constraints to maintain persistent monitoring ref [36]. For continuous, real-time SHM, optimization may also reflect computational throughput and interpretability requirements, since sensor configurations that generate richer data are not always preferable if they exceed onboard or remote processing capabilities ref [15].

Overall, these formulations shift SHM design toward multi-objective optimization in which reliability gain, uncertainty reduction, lifecycle utility, energy sustainability, and cyber-physical feasibility are jointly considered. This broader perspective is essential for deployable SHM systems, especially when monitoring outcomes are directly linked to asset management decisions and safety assurance ref [15], ref [28], ref [33], ref [35], ref [56].

subsections.section_title: Optimization Problem Formulations for Sensor Placement and SHM Design
subsections.subsection_title: Optimization Problem Formulations for Sensor Placement and SHM Design - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A distinct class of optimization formulations in sensor placement and SHM design is driven by sparsity and resource minimization. Here, the design variables are not only sensor locations, but also the number of active channels, interrogation schedules, and sensing modalities, with objectives such as minimizing sensor count, communication burden, or actuation events while preserving damage detectability or reconstruction fidelity. Compressive-sensing-oriented formulations are representative: they exploit signal sparsity to recover structural response or damage features from under-sampled measurements, thereby converting placement into a joint sensing-and-reconstruction problem constrained by coherence, recoverability, and classification performance rather than by dense observability alone ref [24]. Similar sparse design logic appears in ultrasonic array synthesis, where aperture elements are selected to retain imaging capability with fewer transducers, effectively posing placement as a combinatorial trade-off between inspection coverage and hardware economy ref [30].

In practice, these sparse formulations are tightly coupled with deployability constraints. Real-world SHM implementations must account for inaccessible locations, wiring complexity, maintenance burden, power availability, and robustness of communication and embedded hardware, so optimization problems often include explicit penalties or feasibility constraints for installation and lifecycle operation ref [26], ref [39]. This is especially important in wireless or hierarchical networks, where local processing, duty cycling, and distributed actuation alter the effective cost of each sensing node; consequently, placement is often optimized jointly with network architecture and sensing hierarchy rather than treated as a purely geometric selection problem ref [43]. Passive and low-power sensing technologies, including RFID-based strain sensing, further motivate formulations that maximize information per unit energy or per interrogation opportunity, particularly when continuous high-rate acquisition is infeasible ref [53].

Broader SHM system design also increasingly incorporates power-awareness and adaptive learning into the optimization statement. Energy-harvesting-enabled SHM motivates objectives that balance sensing benefit against harvested-energy budgets, yielding formulations with energy-neutrality constraints and time-varying sensing schedules instead of static placement alone ref [20]. Likewise, active-learning and Bayesian model-updating frameworks support sequential sensor selection, in which new measurements are chosen to reduce model uncertainty most efficiently, often through surrogate models such as Kriging and probabilistic inference ref [21]. Taken together, these studies shift the formulation from classical one-shot optimal placement toward integrated sparse, adaptive, and resource-constrained SHM co-design ref [24], ref [26], ref [20].

subsections.section_title: Optimization Problem Formulations for Sensor Placement and SHM Design
subsections.subsection_title: Optimization Problem Formulations for Sensor Placement and SHM Design - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A final class of formulations extends optimal sensor placement beyond estimation accuracy toward deployable SHM system design under resource and infrastructure constraints. In these problems, the objective is typically multi-criteria: maximize identifiability or damage sensitivity while minimizing power demand, communication burden, maintenance frequency, and lifecycle cost. Reviews of sensor placement and SHM system design consistently note that feasible optima are shaped by accessibility, installation practicality, network topology, and environmental exposure rather than information metrics alone ref [14], ref [30].

For wireless and distributed SHM, optimization variables often include not only sensor locations but also sampling schedules, transmission policies, and node roles. IoT-oriented SHM frameworks motivate formulations in which latency, bandwidth, interoperability, and edge/cloud partitioning appear explicitly as constraints or secondary objectives ref [15]. Likewise, ultra-low-power sensing and energy-harvesting studies encourage energy-aware formulations that couple placement with duty cycling and harvested-power availability, so that coverage or detectability must be achieved within strict energy budgets over long monitoring horizons ref [49], ref [51]. These considerations are especially important when dense deployments are attractive diagnostically but unsustainable operationally ref [30].

Such constrained formulations are commonly solved as combinatorial or evolutionary multi-objective problems. Evolutionary computation is particularly suitable when the design space mixes discrete placement decisions with nonlinear sensing and networking constraints ref [56]. Domain-specific performance indices can also be embedded into these broader formulations; for example, modal strain energy, modal assurance distribution, and related seismic or vibration-based indicators provide sensitivity-driven objective terms, while PSO and other metaheuristics search for layouts that remain practical under real deployment restrictions ref [55], ref [48], ref [14]. Overall, this formulation perspective reframes sensor placement as a system co-design problem balancing structural observability with autonomy, robustness, and implementability ref [15], ref [49].

subsections.section_title: Classes of Optimization Algorithms for Structural Health Monitoring
subsections.subsection_title: Classes of Optimization Algorithms for Structural Health Monitoring - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A useful starting point for classifying optimization in structural health monitoring (SHM) and optimal sensor placement (OSP) is the distinction between deterministic and stochastic search. Deterministic methods typically exploit explicit problem structure, gradients, convex surrogates, or sequential ranking rules, and are most effective when the objective and constraints are smooth, low- to moderate-dimensional, and computationally tractable. By contrast, SHM design tasks often involve discrete sensor-selection variables, multimodal objective landscapes, model uncertainty, and coupled constraints on cost, coverage, and identifiability, which motivates broader use of heuristic and metaheuristic search strategies ref [16], ref [55], ref [26].

Within OSP, deterministic formulations remain important because they provide interpretable baselines and can yield efficient solutions for criteria derived from modal information, Fisher information, or observability measures. However, review studies consistently note their sensitivity to initialization, simplifications of the structural model, and reduced robustness when the search space becomes combinatorial or when multiple competing objectives must be balanced simultaneously ref [16], ref [55]. Comparative SHM algorithm studies further suggest that performance can vary substantially across benchmark data sets, reinforcing that no single optimizer is uniformly best across sensing, feature-selection, and damage-detection tasks ref [28].

These limitations have driven increasing interest in optimization frameworks that tolerate high-dimensional data and nonconvex design spaces, especially when paired with machine learning pipelines for feature extraction, classification, or model updating. Recent overviews emphasize that modern SHM increasingly operates in data-rich settings where optimization must interact with learning models, sparse measurements, and heterogeneous sensing modalities ref [59], ref [34]. This trend is reflected in data-driven formulations such as support vector machine models tuned by optimization routines for damage detection, as well as application-specific schemes that couple physics-based indicators with population-based search, including teaching-learning-based optimization ref [27], ref [46]. Accordingly, the algorithm classes reviewed in the following subsections should be understood not as isolated categories, but as progressively richer responses to the scale, uncertainty, and hybrid physics-data character of contemporary SHM ref [26], ref [55].

subsections.section_title: Classes of Optimization Algorithms for Structural Health Monitoring
subsections.subsection_title: Classes of Optimization Algorithms for Structural Health Monitoring - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A distinct class within SHM optimization is learning-assisted optimization, where machine learning models are used either to replace expensive physics-based evaluations or to guide search toward informative sensing configurations and damage-sensitive features. Reviews of data-driven SHM consistently show that supervised, unsupervised, and deep architectures are increasingly coupled with signal processing and feature engineering to reduce computational burden while preserving diagnostic accuracy in large-scale monitoring problems ref [11], ref [36], ref [66]. In the context of optimal sensor placement, these methods are especially attractive when the objective depends on high-dimensional vibration, impedance, or multimodal response data that are costly to evaluate repeatedly.

Several studies illustrate the diversity of such learning mechanisms. Support-vector formulations combined with autoregressive representations have been used to learn discriminative damage indicators directly from structural time series, effectively embedding classification capability into the optimization loop ref [37]. Fuzzy pattern recognition and fuzzy clustering approaches similarly support optimization under ambiguity by grouping modal or damage signatures when labels are scarce or noise is significant ref [34], ref [24]. More recent feature-fusion and hybrid deep-learning pipelines further expand this role by automatically extracting hierarchical representations from heterogeneous SHM data, which can improve objective surrogates for sensor selection and monitoring design ref [28]. Automatic operational modal analysis based on machine learning also demonstrates how learned modal identification can accelerate iterative placement and model-updating procedures in practical bridge applications ref [54].

Despite these advantages, learning-assisted optimization inherits important limitations. Its performance depends strongly on data representativeness, feature stability across environmental and operational variability, and the availability of sufficiently rich training sets ref [11], ref [36]. Consequently, these methods are most effective when integrated with domain knowledge, signal processing, and uncertainty-aware validation rather than used as stand-alone optimizers ref [66], ref [54].

subsections.section_title: Classes of Optimization Algorithms for Structural Health Monitoring
subsections.subsection_title: Classes of Optimization Algorithms for Structural Health Monitoring - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
Learning-assisted optimization has emerged as a distinct class for SHM and OSP when objective evaluations are expensive, noisy, or strongly data dependent. Rather than replacing optimization, machine learning is typically used to construct surrogate fitness models, extract compact damage-sensitive features, or guide adaptive search toward promising sensing layouts and decision variables. This paradigm is particularly relevant in high-dimensional SHM settings, where robust dimensionality reduction can suppress redundancy before optimization and thereby improve tractability and stability of the design process ref [17], ref [53].

Deep learning has strengthened this class by providing end-to-end mappings from heterogeneous sensor data to damage indicators, which can then serve as optimization objectives or constraints. Representative studies demonstrate real-time crack detection and localization from strain-gauge measurements, deep-learning-based crack identification in gas-turbine components, and online SHM pipelines combining model order reduction with deep networks for rapid monitoring updates ref [22], ref [22], ref [24]. In practical infrastructure applications, data-driven interpretation of bridge responses under thermal and traffic effects and machine-learning-based pavement monitoring further show how learned models can accommodate operational variability that is difficult to encode analytically ref [37], ref [49].

The main strengths of learning-assisted optimization are computational acceleration, improved handling of nonlinear response manifolds, and better scalability to multimodal sensor data. However, these methods inherit limitations from training data quality, domain shift, labeling costs, and reduced interpretability, especially when optimized sensor layouts are tied to a specific operational regime. Accordingly, recent reviews at the SHM–NDE interface emphasize that machine learning is most effective when embedded within physics-aware workflows, with dimensionality control, reduced-order modeling, and careful validation used to preserve generalization and reliability ref [53], ref [17], ref [24].

subsections.section_title: Classes of Optimization Algorithms for Structural Health Monitoring
subsections.subsection_title: Classes of Optimization Algorithms for Structural Health Monitoring - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
Learning-assisted optimization forms a distinct class in SHM and OSP because it does not replace optimization, but augments it with data-driven surrogates, adaptive sampling, or predictive models that reduce evaluation cost and improve decision quality in nonlinear, high-dimensional design spaces. In this family, machine learning models are used to approximate expensive structural responses, infer damage-sensitive features, or guide the search toward informative sensing and updating actions rather than relying only on repeated full-order analyses ref [21], ref [51].

A representative mechanism is active learning coupled with probabilistic surrogate modeling. The Kriging-Bayesian framework for multisensory structural model updating shows how adaptive sample selection can focus computations on the most informative regions of the parameter space, thereby improving calibration efficiency under uncertainty ref [21]. Related adaptive-learning damage estimation strategies likewise indicate that iterative data acquisition and model refinement can support damage identification when measurements are sparse or evolving, which is especially relevant to sequential sensor deployment and inspection planning ref [10].

Deep and hybrid learning models further support optimization-oriented SHM by learning complex mappings from raw sensing data to health indicators, reducing the need for handcrafted objective surrogates. Reviews of AI-based SHM emphasize that neural, probabilistic, and pattern-recognition models are increasingly embedded within broader decision pipelines for sensor management and diagnosis ref [51]. Application studies, including temperature-robust ultrasonic guided-wave classification, CNN-LSTM prediction of electromechanical impedance signals, and Gaussian-fitting/LSTM health monitoring of suspension components, illustrate the practical value of learned surrogates under environmental variability and multiscale temporal behavior ref [27], ref [46], ref [58]. Their main limitation is that optimization performance becomes dependent on data quality, domain shift robustness, and interpretability, so learning-assisted methods are most effective when combined with physics-based constraints and uncertainty-aware updating ref [21], ref [27], ref [51].

subsections.section_title: Classes of Optimization Algorithms for Structural Health Monitoring
subsections.subsection_title: Classes of Optimization Algorithms for Structural Health Monitoring - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
Learning-assisted optimization forms a distinct class in SHM because prediction models are not only used for damage classification, but also to guide or replace expensive search steps in design optimization. Statistical pattern recognition established the basis for this shift by framing SHM as feature extraction, novelty detection, and decision-making under uncertainty, thereby enabling optimization to operate on learned damage-sensitive representations rather than raw responses alone [17]. Support vector machine and neural-network formulations further demonstrated how supervised learners can map vibration, image, or video features to structural states with low online latency, making them attractive as surrogate evaluators within iterative sensor-layout and model-updating loops [4], [33].

Recent deep-learning studies reinforce this trend. Convolutional neural networks applied to encoded time-series images show how high-dimensional sensing data can be compressed into discriminative features for rapid condition assessment, which is especially useful when optimization must repeatedly assess candidate sensing configurations or damage scenarios [3]. In parallel, hybrid updating frameworks that exploit long-term monitoring data illustrate a broader learning-assisted paradigm: optimization is coupled with data-driven inference to calibrate model parameters and deterioration trajectories more efficiently than purely physics-based search [12].

In practice, learning-assisted optimization in SHM is rarely standalone; it is usually embedded in hybrid pipelines with evolutionary or swarm search. Examples include PSO-assisted modal strain energy methods for damage identification and broader evolutionary computation frameworks for critical infrastructure, where learning modules accelerate fitness estimation, filter candidate solutions, or improve robustness under noisy field data [6], [56]. For OSP specifically, these methods are most promising when combined with classical placement criteria and system-identification constraints, although their performance still depends strongly on training data quality, interpretability, and generalization across operational variability [14].

subsections.section_title: Data-Driven, Physics-Guided, and Uncertainty-Aware SHM Optimization
subsections.subsection_title: Data-Driven, Physics-Guided, and Uncertainty-Aware SHM Optimization - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A central trend in modern SHM optimization is the shift from purely model-based sensor deployment toward data-centric designs that explicitly account for downstream learning tasks. Reviews on big-data-enabled bridge monitoring and SHM data science emphasize that optimal sensor placement is increasingly judged by its impact on feature quality, data richness, scalability, and decision support rather than by modal observability alone ref [3], ref [10]. In this setting, optimization must co-design sensing layouts with analytics pipelines, including feature extraction, dimensionality reduction, and classifier/regressor performance under high-dimensional and heterogeneous data streams ref [86], ref [34].

Machine-learning-driven SHM also changes the objective functions used in optimization. Instead of maximizing classical information metrics only, sensor layouts can be selected to improve damage separability, generalization accuracy, and robustness of data-driven models such as support vector machines and related optimized classifiers ref [27]. This perspective is consistent with broader surveys showing that SHM learning systems are sensitive to sparse labels, class imbalance, and nonstationary operating conditions, which makes sensor placement an integral part of model training and validation rather than a preprocessing step ref [86], ref [10], ref [34].

However, data-driven optimization is only reliable when environmental and operational variability is embedded in the design loop. Temperature, loading, and other operational effects can dominate Lamb-wave and vibration features, potentially causing optimized layouts to overfit laboratory conditions ref [30]. Domain adaptation has therefore emerged as a key complement, allowing sensor and model configurations to remain informative under domain shift between baseline and field data, structures, or seasons ref [51]. For this reason, recent sensor-placement reviews argue for integrated formulations that jointly optimize sensing, learning, and transfer robustness, especially for long-term bridge and infrastructure monitoring in noisy real environments ref [16], ref [3].

subsections.section_title: Data-Driven, Physics-Guided, and Uncertainty-Aware SHM Optimization
subsections.subsection_title: Data-Driven, Physics-Guided, and Uncertainty-Aware SHM Optimization - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central trend in modern SHM optimization is the tight coupling between sensor placement and downstream data-driven inference. Rather than maximizing only observability or modal independence, optimization is increasingly framed around predictive utility: placements are evaluated by their ability to support damage classification, response reconstruction, feature fusion, and automated modal identification under noisy field conditions. Reviews of machine-learning-based SHM and structural dynamics show that this shift moves optimal sensor placement toward task-aware criteria linked to classification robustness, feature separability, and generalization performance ref [66], ref [11], ref [36].

Recent deep-learning studies further reinforce this perspective. Densely connected convolutional networks for dynamic response reconstruction suggest that sparse measurements can be strategically positioned to recover unmeasured structural states, turning placement into a learned sensing-and-reconstruction problem ref [15]. Hybrid deep-learning and feature-fusion frameworks similarly imply that heterogeneous sensor configurations should be optimized jointly with multimodal feature extraction pipelines rather than in isolation ref [28]. In infrastructure applications, transfer-learning-based response estimation for dams highlights the importance of optimizing sensor layouts for cross-structure knowledge transfer and domain adaptation when labeled damage data are limited ref [25].

From an uncertainty-aware standpoint, these developments indicate that optimization should account for data drift, environmental variability, and imperfect labels by embedding validation on real monitoring tasks. Machine-learning-based automatic operational modal analysis for masonry arch bridges demonstrates how analytics quality depends on measurement informativeness under ambient excitation ref [54], while SHM data-fusion approaches for in-situ life prognosis of composite structures show that prognostic value emerges from coordinated sensing, fusion, and decision support ref [55]. Consequently, data-driven SHM optimization is evolving from static geometry-based design toward adaptive, analytics-informed, and fusion-oriented sensor deployment strategies ref [66], ref [11], ref [36].

subsections.section_title: Data-Driven, Physics-Guided, and Uncertainty-Aware SHM Optimization
subsections.subsection_title: Data-Driven, Physics-Guided, and Uncertainty-Aware SHM Optimization - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central trend in modern SHM optimization is the coupling of sensor configuration with feature learning under strong environmental and operational variability. Robust dimensionality-reduction strategies help optimization focus on damage-sensitive latent variables while suppressing nuisance variations and redundancy, which is particularly important when sensor budgets are limited and field measurements are noisy ref [17]. In bridge monitoring, data-driven interpretation of combined thermal and traffic responses further shows that optimal sensing and analytics cannot be designed independently; instead, placement should target locations that improve separability between operational effects and genuine structural change ref [37].

Physics-guided learning provides an important bridge between purely statistical models and deployable SHM systems. Reduced-order models combined with deep learning enable online monitoring with lower computational cost, suggesting that optimization should jointly consider sensor placement, state-reconstruction fidelity, and real-time inference constraints ref [24]. This logic is consistent with model-based SHM in ship hulls, where structural mechanics models constrain damage inference and make sparse measurements more informative ref [50]. At a broader interface, machine learning and NDE research indicates that hybrid pipelines are most effective when data-driven classifiers are informed by sensing physics, inspection modalities, and damage mechanisms rather than trained as black boxes ref [53].

Uncertainty-aware optimization extends this integration from detection to decision-making. In life-cycle assessment of ship structures, SHM data are embedded in uncertain performance and maintenance models, implying that optimal sensor layouts should be evaluated by their value for reliability updating and risk-informed intervention planning, not only by immediate damage-classification accuracy ref [33]. This perspective aligns with evolving SHM reliability metrics based on probability of detection, localization, and sizing, which provide more decision-relevant objectives for optimization under uncertainty ref [56]. Overall, the emerging direction is to optimize sensing systems against downstream tasks in digital-twin updating, prognosis, and asset management, using data-driven models that remain constrained by physics and explicitly calibrated for uncertainty ref [24], ref [33], ref [50].

subsections.section_title: Data-Driven, Physics-Guided, and Uncertainty-Aware SHM Optimization
subsections.subsection_title: Data-Driven, Physics-Guided, and Uncertainty-Aware SHM Optimization - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A central theme in uncertainty-aware SHM optimization is the use of adaptive learning to decide what data should be acquired next, where sensors should be emphasized, and how models should be updated as evidence accumulates. Adaptive damage estimation frameworks illustrate how sequential learning can refine diagnostic accuracy while reducing redundant measurements, making optimization intrinsically data-acquisition aware rather than purely geometry based ref [10]. In parallel, active learning model updating with Kriging surrogates and Bayesian inference shows that multisensory systems can be reconfigured around the most informative observations, linking optimal sensing to posterior uncertainty reduction in both parameters and predictions ref [21].

Robustness to environmental and operational variability is equally critical. Temperature-induced shifts can severely distort guided-wave features, and comparative evaluations of machine-learning classifiers under varying thermal conditions demonstrate that sensor deployment and feature-selection strategies must be optimized jointly with compensation models to preserve transferability in field settings ref [27]. Statistical monitoring approaches based on autoregressive coefficients and Hotelling's T2 charts further highlight that uncertainty-aware optimization should include baseline variability, threshold design, and false-alarm control, not only damage sensitivity ref [38]. Hybrid sequence models such as CNN-LSTM and LSTM integrated with probabilistic signal fitting also indicate that temporal prediction quality depends on placing sensors where degradation signatures remain stable enough for forecasting under noisy conditions ref [46], ref [58].

Physics guidance remains essential when optimization moves from detection to prognosis and decision support. Physical model-based prognostics frameworks connect SHM data to degradation evolution and maintenance scheduling, providing a mechanism to constrain data-driven learners with mechanically meaningful state transitions ref [35]. Likewise, reliability-based bridge load-carrying capacity assessment combines monitored response with nonlinear analysis to propagate uncertainty from measurements to safety metrics, clarifying that optimal sensor layouts should be judged by their value for reliability updating and predictive maintenance rather than by information gain alone ref [47].

subsections.section_title: Data-Driven, Physics-Guided, and Uncertainty-Aware SHM Optimization
subsections.subsection_title: Data-Driven, Physics-Guided, and Uncertainty-Aware SHM Optimization - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A salient direction in SHM optimization is the closed-loop integration of data-driven inference with physics-based models and long-term monitoring, where sensor configuration, model updating, and damage diagnosis are optimized jointly rather than sequentially. Advanced finite-element representations of large bridges provide the physics backbone for this integration, enabling sensor data to calibrate structural states and boundary-condition uncertainties in digital-twin-like workflows ref [33]. In parallel, hybrid model-updating strategies using long-term monitoring data show how deterioration assessment can be improved when optimization is used to reconcile measured responses with evolving structural parameters under environmental and operational variability ref [12]. Similar hybrid condition-assessment frameworks for cable-stayed bridges further indicate that optimization must balance feature informativeness, model fidelity, and monitoring cost across heterogeneous sensing modalities ref [55].

On the data-driven side, optimization increasingly targets feature representations and classifier robustness under noisy field data and domain shift. Early statistical pattern-recognition formulations established the basis for novelty detection, outlier handling, and damage-sensitive feature selection under uncertain operating conditions ref [17]. Subsequent vibration-based support vector machine approaches demonstrated that optimization of kernels, features, and decision boundaries can materially affect damage discrimination performance ref [82], while convolutional neural network pipelines that encode vibration time series into images illustrate how representation learning can reduce manual feature engineering but shift the optimization burden toward data curation, architecture choice, and sensor placement adequacy ref [95]. Video-based ANN monitoring extends this trend by showing that sensing topology may also include noncontact modalities, raising new optimization questions related to viewpoint selection, occlusion, and real-time inference constraints ref [33].

Uncertainty-aware SHM optimization therefore benefits from hybrid search strategies that couple probabilistic reasoning with global optimization. Evolutionary computation has been used to explore high-dimensional design spaces in critical-infrastructure monitoring, especially where discrete sensor-placement decisions interact with nonlinear damage models and sparse observations ref [56]. At the same time, statistical pattern-recognition and hybrid bridge-assessment studies suggest that robust solutions are those that remain informative under model mismatch, missing data, and changing operational regimes rather than only under nominal simulations ref [17], ref [55]. Collectively, these works indicate that modern SHM optimization should be framed as a multi-objective problem spanning prediction accuracy, physical consistency, adaptability, and uncertainty resilience ref [33], ref [12].

subsections.section_title: Application Domains and Comparative Performance Across Structural Systems
subsections.subsection_title: Application Domains and Comparative Performance Across Structural Systems - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Comparative evidence across structural systems shows that optimization objectives are strongly domain-dependent. In bridges, sensor placement is commonly driven by network-scale condition assessment, damage localization under operational variability, and the integration of data analytics with long-term monitoring streams, which favors hybrid objective functions balancing observability, redundancy, and lifecycle decision support ref [98], ref [16]. By contrast, aircraft composite structures emphasize high-resolution detection of barely visible impact damage, delamination, and fatigue progression, so optimization is more tightly coupled to guided-wave coverage, sparse transducer layouts, weight constraints, and onboard power limitations ref [84], ref [16].

Wind energy structures occupy an intermediate position: blades require distributed sensing for strain, acoustic, vibration, and cure-state tracking over large anisotropic components, while towers and nacelle subsystems often prioritize durability monitoring under highly nonstationary environmental loading ref [24], ref [41], ref [54]. Reviews consistently note that no single algorithm dominates across these cases; instead, performance depends on the match between search strategy and sensing physics, with combinatorial placement methods and metaheuristics being most valuable when coverage, accessibility, and multi-damage sensitivity must be handled simultaneously ref [16], ref [24], ref [41].

Other domains further reinforce this application specificity. Railway monitoring has leaned heavily on fiber-optic sensing because long linear assets benefit from multiplexing, electromagnetic immunity, and continuous strain/temperature measurements, shifting optimization toward sensor spacing, interrogation range, and maintenance economics rather than only modal identifiability ref [29]. Heritage buildings present a different trade space: minimally invasive deployment, sparse labels, and heterogeneous masonry behavior make machine-learning-assisted monitoring attractive, but also increase the importance of robust feature selection and conservative placement strategies that respect architectural constraints ref [36]. Overall, the literature suggests that comparative algorithm performance is best interpreted within each structural class rather than generalized universally from one domain to another ref [84], ref [98], ref [29], ref [36].

subsections.section_title: Application Domains and Comparative Performance Across Structural Systems
subsections.subsection_title: Application Domains and Comparative Performance Across Structural Systems - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Infrastructure classes with constrained access and heterogeneous materials—such as tunnels, wind turbines, timber systems, and heritage assets—tend to shift optimization priorities away from purely modal identifiability toward robustness, coverage, and sensing survivability. In tunnels, distributed optical fiber sensing is attractive because the objective is continuous strain-field coverage under nearby construction disturbances rather than sparse localization at a few candidate points, which alters optimal sensor placement from discrete combinatorial selection to path design and redundancy allocation ref [104]. A similar trend appears in wind energy structures, where large spatial gradients, rotating components, and harsh offshore environments make durability, power supply, and maintenance logistics central optimization constraints alongside diagnostic sensitivity ref [14], ref [45], ref [52].

For wind turbines specifically, comparative evidence suggests that algorithm performance depends strongly on subsystem and sensing modality. Blade and tower monitoring often favor fiber Bragg grating and distributed strain layouts because they support lightweight integration and multiplexing, but offshore support structures additionally require strategies that balance corrosion/fatigue observability with reliability of long-term deployment ref [45], ref [52]. Reviews from China also emphasize that practical bottlenecks are less about the absence of detection algorithms than about integrating sensing, transmission, and decision layers into cost-effective full-life systems, implying that optimization should be formulated as a multi-objective problem coupling information gain with maintainability and lifecycle risk ref [14].

For historic and materially diverse structures, optimal monitoring is even more domain-specific. Timber structures require sensor plans tailored to moisture-sensitive degradation, creep, and localized connection damage, so hybrid schemes combining environmental and mechanical indicators are generally more suitable than vibration-only layouts ref [29]. In masonry arch bridges and broader heritage stocks, non-contact or minimally invasive sensing is often preferred; integrated GPR-InSAR approaches and carefully deployed long-span arch bridge monitoring systems illustrate how optimization must trade off diagnostic richness, intrusiveness, and preservation constraints ref [57], ref [20], while Italian heritage case studies further show that monitoring design is governed by conservation priorities as much as by algorithmic detection accuracy ref [30].

subsections.section_title: Application Domains and Comparative Performance Across Structural Systems
subsections.subsection_title: Application Domains and Comparative Performance Across Structural Systems - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
In aerospace composites and bonded repairs, optimization is typically driven by early detection of barely visible damage, adhesive disbonds, and crack growth under severe weight, wiring, and certification constraints. Accordingly, the literature emphasizes active sensing layouts based on piezoelectric transducers and guided-wave interrogation, because Lamb-wave paths can be tailored to maximize coverage of joints, patches, and skin–stiffener interfaces while limiting sensor count ref [34], ref [38]. Studies on patched cracks and composite repairs further show that practical deployment depends not only on detectability but also on maintainability and compatibility with fleet life-extension programs, which narrows the feasible design space for sensor placement and interrogation strategies ref [113], ref [57].

Comparative evidence across aircraft applications suggests that algorithm performance is highly coupled to the sensing modality. Electromechanical impedance approaches are attractive for highly localized monitoring of adhesive disbonds, where optimization often concerns excitation frequency selection and transducer positioning near stress concentrations rather than network-scale observability ref [23]. By contrast, Lamb-wave systems support larger-area coverage but require optimization against anisotropy, boundary reflections, and environmental variability in composite laminates and joints ref [34], ref [38]. Program-level validation in operational military aircraft indicates that successful SHM architectures balance detection performance with robustness, false-alarm control, and integration into structural health and usage monitoring workflows, reinforcing the need for multi-objective formulations beyond pure damage sensitivity ref [13].

A related pattern appears in composite wind turbine blades, where the monitored structure is larger and damage mechanisms include fatigue-driven delamination, debonding, and defect growth over long service intervals. Reviews and experimental blade studies indicate that optimization shifts from dense local arrays toward sparse, durable layouts with sufficient sensitivity to distributed damage over meter-scale components ref [32], ref [46]. Relative to aircraft structures, blade applications face stronger trade-offs among coverage, power/data logistics, and survivability in harsh environments, so comparative performance often favors simpler, more robust sensing schemes even at lower spatial resolution ref [32]. Overall, these domains show that optimization objectives are structure-specific: aircraft SHM prioritizes high-resolution localization in critical joints and repairs, whereas blade monitoring prioritizes scalable coverage and long-term reliability ref [113], ref [46], ref [57].

subsections.section_title: Application Domains and Comparative Performance Across Structural Systems
subsections.subsection_title: Application Domains and Comparative Performance Across Structural Systems - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
For civil infrastructure beyond canonical bridge case studies, optimization objectives are strongly shaped by accessibility, environmental variability, and the dominant damage mechanism. In dams, long-term assessment must separate thermal, hydrostatic, and seasonal effects from genuine structural anomalies, which tends to favor sensor layouts optimized for robustness to environmental confounding rather than only modal identifiability ref [31]. In railway tunnels and retrofitted buildings, by contrast, predictive maintenance and post-intervention verification often prioritize distributed observation of localized deformation, vibration change, and serviceability indicators under sparse instrumentation budgets ref [33], ref [41].

Bridges remain the most mature comparison domain, and the literature shows that algorithm performance depends heavily on sensing modality. Conventional vibration-based networks support global condition assessment and system-level model updating, while acoustic emission approaches are more sensitive to active cracking and prestress-related fracture processes, as illustrated in a prestressed concrete bridge tested to failure ref [50], ref [17]. Remote sensing via synthetic aperture radar further shifts the optimization problem toward revisit frequency, line-of-sight coverage, and fusion with in-situ sensors, rather than dense physical deployment alone ref [23].

Linear transportation and energy assets impose yet another optimization regime. For rails, ultrasonic guided waves are attractive because relatively sparse transducer placement can interrogate long propagation paths, but algorithm choice must explicitly handle dispersion, boundary reflections, and defect localization uncertainty ref [56]. In pipelines and wind turbines, review evidence similarly indicates that optimal placement is governed by long-range coverage, harsh environments, and cost-sensitive maintenance logistics, encouraging hybrid strategies that combine local high-fidelity sensors with broader condition-screening systems ref [45]. Overall, comparative results across these structural systems suggest that no single optimization algorithm dominates universally; performance is domain-dependent and tightly coupled to physics, sensing range, and operational constraints ref [31], ref [45], ref [50].

subsections.section_title: Application Domains and Comparative Performance Across Structural Systems
subsections.subsection_title: Application Domains and Comparative Performance Across Structural Systems - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A final cross-domain group comprises rotating machinery, aerospace platforms, heritage assets, and transport corridors, where optimization problems are strongly constrained by accessibility, safety certification, and sparse observability. In turbine engines, microwave blade-tip-clearance sensing emphasizes high-rate, localized measurements under extreme operating conditions rather than dense sensor deployment, shifting optimization toward survivability and diagnostic sensitivity per channel rather than coverage alone ref [10]. In airframes, on-board SHM is motivated by maintenance avoidance, so algorithmic choices are evaluated by false-alarm control, decision reliability, and integration with usage-based maintenance workflows ref [21]. More broadly, evolutionary computation has been proposed for critical infrastructure SHM as a flexible framework for multi-objective trade-offs, although its practical value depends on domain-specific sensing constraints and model fidelity ref [56].

Wind-energy applications illustrate how structural form and sensing modality shape comparative performance. Experimental monitoring of wind turbine blades shows that blade-scale SHM must accommodate composite anisotropy, rotating operational variability, and distributed damage scenarios ref [38]. Acoustic-array approaches offer improved localization of impact or defect-related acoustic events over single-sensor schemes, but they also introduce array-geometry and noise-robustness optimization challenges ref [44]. These studies suggest that for blades, optimization is less about a universal best algorithm and more about matching objective functions to wave propagation, rotating boundary conditions, and maintenance economics ref [38], ref [44].

For culturally significant and geographically extended assets, optimization objectives broaden further. In heritage buildings, SHM strategies are typically constrained by reversibility, minimal invasiveness, and compatibility with conservation practice; consequently, optimal placement favors low-intrusion sensing and long-term interpretation rather than dense actuation-heavy layouts ref [23]. For railway viaducts monitored by ground-based radar interferometry, the main issues concern line-of-sight dependence, environmental disturbance, and interpretation of displacement fields, indicating that remote-sensing configurations can outperform contact networks in accessibility but may underperform for localized damage characterization ref [39]. Across these domains, the literature points to a common conclusion: the best-performing optimization strategy is highly application-specific and must co-design sensor type, placement, and decision objective with the governing damage mechanism ref [10], ref [21], ref [23], ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Benchmarking, Deployment Challenges, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Benchmarking, Deployment Challenges, and Future Research Directions - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A first bottleneck to assessing optimization algorithms for structural health monitoring (SHM) and optimal sensor placement is the weakness of current benchmarking practice. Reviews of SHM and OSP repeatedly note that methods are often validated on different structures, sensor budgets, noise levels, and objective functions, making cross-paper comparison unreliable ref [16], ref [26], ref [55]. As a result, reported gains for genetic algorithms, particle swarm variants, Bayesian schemes, or learning-based optimizers frequently reflect problem setup rather than intrinsic algorithmic superiority.

The literature therefore points to a need for standardized, openly documented benchmark tasks that couple realistic sensing constraints with common evaluation protocols. Algorithm-comparison studies using standard data sets show the value of fixed baselines, identical training/testing splits, and transparent performance reporting ref [28]. Bridge-scale benchmark problems built from monitored data of actual infrastructure are especially important because they expose environmental variability, missing data, and operational uncertainty that are absent in many simulated studies ref [44]. This is particularly relevant for machine-learning-assisted optimization, whose apparent performance can degrade sharply under distribution shift; domain adaptation studies explicitly show that transfer across structures or operating conditions remains nontrivial ref [51], while broader ML reviews warn against overclaiming generalization from narrow laboratory data ref [34].

From a deployment perspective, benchmarking must also reflect industrial decision criteria. Practical adoption reviews emphasize that SHM algorithms are rarely accepted on the basis of detection accuracy alone; maintainability, interpretability, certification readiness, computational burden, and lifecycle value are equally important ref [15], ref [26]. Accordingly, future benchmarks for optimization-enabled SHM should report not only objective-function optima, but also robustness to sensor faults, repeatability across runs, sensitivity to modeling assumptions, and downstream maintenance impact. Such benchmark design would narrow the research-to-deployment gap and provide a more credible basis for comparing optimization strategies in realistic SHM pipelines ref [15], ref [16], ref [28].

subsections.section_title: Benchmarking, Deployment Challenges, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Benchmarking, Deployment Challenges, and Future Research Directions - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central deployment challenge for optimization-enabled SHM is the mismatch between algorithmic assumptions and field operating conditions. Reviews of vibration-based SHM and technical codes show that practical systems must satisfy requirements on measurement quality, calibration, traceability, and decision accountability that are rarely embedded in optimization studies ref [10]. From a benchmarking perspective, the Structural Health Monitoring Benchmark Problem demonstrated the value of controlled experimental phases for comparing damage detection and sensor-layout strategies, but it also highlighted that success on curated testbeds does not automatically translate to robustness under environmental variability, incomplete instrumentation, and changing boundary conditions ref [17].

Field deployments further reveal integration barriers at the system level. Case studies on long-span arch bridges and multi-story buildings report that communication reliability, power management, sensor maintenance, and data governance often dominate lifecycle cost, constraining the practical value of computationally optimal placements ref [20], ref [56]. Software frameworks such as MOVA/MOSS illustrate that industrial adoption depends not only on optimization performance, but on interoperable workflows for data ingestion, visualization, diagnostics, and decision support ref [51]. Similar conclusions emerge from broader discussions on SHM prescription and implementation, which argue that optimization must be tied to actionable maintenance objectives rather than abstract detectability metrics alone ref [46].

These issues point to several research priorities. First, benchmarking should move toward end-to-end evaluation, including false-alarm behavior, maintainability, missing-data resilience, and compatibility with technical codes ref [10], ref [46]. Second, optimization for sensor placement should explicitly account for cyber-physical integration, especially where SHM is linked with intelligent transportation systems and networked bridge management platforms ref [50]. Third, machine-learning-based optimization pipelines require validation under real deployment drift, not only offline accuracy, as emphasized in reviews of ML for buildings and bridges ref [36]. A credible roadmap therefore combines benchmark standardization, software interoperability, code-aware validation, and lifecycle-oriented objective functions ref [17], ref [20], ref [50], ref [51].

subsections.section_title: Benchmarking, Deployment Challenges, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Benchmarking, Deployment Challenges, and Future Research Directions - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central deployment challenge for optimization-enabled SHM is the gap between benchmark success and field robustness. Community benchmark studies have been valuable for comparing damage-identification pipelines under controlled conditions, including benchmark buildings and experimental testbeds, but they often simplify environmental variability, sensing failures, and maintenance constraints that dominate real operations ref [9], ref [44]. Broader state-of-the-art assessments similarly note that many SHM methods remain validated on limited scenarios, making cross-study comparison difficult and hindering confidence in optimized sensor layouts or decision thresholds when transferred to practice ref [10].

For industrial adoption, optimization must therefore be assessed together with data quality management, real-time interpretability, and certifiable reliability. Continuous monitoring systems generate heterogeneous streaming data, and practical value depends on timely interpretation rather than offline accuracy alone ref [15]. In wireless and resource-constrained deployments, sensor fault management is not a peripheral issue: optimization routines that ignore missing, drifting, or corrupted sensors can produce brittle placement or diagnosis strategies ref [16]. Aerospace validation studies further show that acceptance depends on demonstrating performance within operational workflows, maintenance doctrines, and safety cases, not merely algorithmic superiority on laboratory datasets ref [13].

Future benchmarking should move beyond single-objective detection accuracy toward reproducible, mission-oriented protocols that jointly evaluate detection, localization, sizing, false alarms, latency, resilience to sensor faults, and lifecycle cost. Reliability-oriented metrics such as probability of detection, localization, and sizing provide a stronger basis for certification and risk-informed optimization than raw classification scores alone ref [56]. At the same time, emerging machine-learning-based SHM should be benchmarked under domain shift, sparse labels, and NDE-informed ground truth to reflect realistic deployment conditions ref [53]. A credible roadmap is thus to couple open benchmark datasets with operational validation campaigns and reliability metrics that are explicitly aligned with end-user decisions ref [44], ref [13], ref [56].

subsections.section_title: Benchmarking, Deployment Challenges, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Benchmarking, Deployment Challenges, and Future Research Directions - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A central deployment challenge for optimization-enabled SHM is the gap between benchmark success and field robustness. Reviews of benchmark studies show that many algorithms are still validated on canonical damage cases, limited sensor faults, and comparatively clean operating conditions, which constrains conclusions about scalability and transferability to real assets ref [16], ref [25]. This is particularly problematic for optimal sensor placement, where designs tuned to idealized finite-element models may degrade under modeling error, installation constraints, or changing boundary conditions in service ref [25], ref [39].

Practical implementation further depends on end-to-end system issues that are often outside the optimization objective itself: power supply, communication reliability, data governance, maintenance burden, cyber-physical integration, and interoperability with cloud or enterprise platforms ref [27], ref [25]. Large-scale bridge and infrastructure reviews similarly note that sparse access, harsh environments, calibration drift, and heterogeneous sensing modalities can dominate lifecycle cost and reliability, even when the underlying monitoring algorithm is accurate ref [50], ref [39]. Consequently, benchmarking should move beyond detection accuracy alone toward deployability-oriented metrics such as uptime, false-alarm burden, resilience to missing data, computational latency, and operator interpretability ref [16], ref [50].

Future research should therefore couple optimization with reliability and decision frameworks. Bridge assessment studies indicate that SHM becomes more actionable when measurements are linked to reliability-based capacity evaluation and maintenance prioritization rather than treated as isolated diagnostics ref [47]. A useful roadmap is to establish multi-tier benchmarks that combine controlled benchmark structures, long-term field data, and sensor-to-cloud operational workflows, enabling reproducible comparison of optimization methods under realistic uncertainty, asset-management objectives, and certification requirements ref [25], ref [27], ref [16].

subsections.section_title: Benchmarking, Deployment Challenges, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Benchmarking, Deployment Challenges, and Future Research Directions - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A forward-looking research agenda for optimization-enabled SHM must move beyond algorithmic accuracy toward deployable, networked, and maintainable systems. Reviews on IoT-enabled SHM emphasize that future optimization should jointly consider sensing, communication, edge/cloud computing, cybersecurity, and data interoperability rather than treating sensor placement as an isolated design problem ref [15]. This systems perspective is especially important in bridge monitoring, where long-term operation, environmental variability, and heterogeneous asset inventories require scalable architectures and standardized data pipelines ref [19].

A second priority is energy-aware and autonomy-oriented optimization. Practical SHM deployments remain constrained by power budgets, wireless transmission costs, and maintenance of distributed sensor nodes; accordingly, optimal sensor placement and scheduling should be co-designed with energy harvesting, duty cycling, and hardware reliability models ref [51], ref [30]. The same deployment logic appears in national and regional SHM programs, where large-scale implementation has been shaped not only by sensing performance but also by infrastructure management practices, standardization efforts, and technology transfer capacity ref [25], ref [46].

Finally, future benchmarking should reward maintenance value and certifiability, not only damage-detection metrics. Aerospace demonstrations show that SHM becomes operationally compelling when optimization supports inspection reduction and maintenance deferral under auditable evidence frameworks ref [21]. This suggests that next-generation benchmarks should incorporate lifecycle cost, false-alarm consequences, uncertainty quantification, and decision impact across critical infrastructure sectors, while leveraging evolutionary and other metaheuristic methods only when their robustness, transparency, and reproducibility can be demonstrated in realistic deployment settings ref [56].
